paragraphes: You know how to cross at a crosswalk. Someone told you when you were small: look both ways before you cross.
Later, someone explained why: cars need time to stop. And an instructor made you practice on your bike, for real.
In a company, everyone also has to learn good security habits. This is called a security awareness program.

decouverte.comme: Knowing that you should use the crosswalk is awareness. Understanding why is education. Practicing with an instructor is training.
decouverte.enVrai: The title of the manual section puts these three words together: awareness, education and training. The manual gives an official definition of the awareness program. The picture stops here: in real life, these three ways of learning mix together.

decouverte.question: A company has the best security tools. Where is its weakest point?
options: The people who work there
The price of its tools
The number of its computers
decouverte.explanation: Tools block technical attacks. But a person who gets tricked can get around all of them. The price and the number of computers do not change that.

decouverte.texte: Lea joins a company. During her first week, she follows an orientation for new employees. She watches an online course (CBT: computer-based training, a lesson you take on a computer). In the hallways, posters remind people of security tips.

cards.question: Official definition: “security awareness program”
cards.answer: A security awareness program is a formal program that includes processes to train users of the potential threats to an organization's information and systems, as well as educates those users on how to handle such threats.
cards.explanation: Two jobs: make the threats known, then teach how to handle them.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness, Education, and Training Program”.

cards.question: A security awareness program is a formal program that includes processes to [[train]] users of the potential threats to an organization's information and systems, as well as [[educates]] those users on how to handle such threats.
cards.answer: A security awareness program is a formal program that includes processes to train users of the potential threats to an organization's information and systems, as well as educates those users on how to handle such threats.
cards.explanation: Two verbs: train (inform) and educates (teach how to handle).

cards.question: A security awareness program is a [[formal program]] that includes processes to [[train users]] of the potential threats to an organization's information and systems, as well as [[educates those users]] on how to handle such threats.
cards.answer: A security awareness program is a formal program that includes processes to train users of the potential threats to an organization's information and systems, as well as educates those users on how to handle such threats.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a formal program, informing the users, teaching them to handle threats.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “security awareness program” from memory.
cards.answer: A security awareness program is a formal program that includes processes to train users of the potential threats to an organization's information and systems, as well as educates those users on how to handle such threats.
cards.explanation: Start with “formal program”, then the two jobs: train and educates.

cards.question: Official definition: the minimum content of a standard program
cards.answer: A standard security awareness program should include, at a minimum, new user orientation, lectures or computer-based trainings (CBTs), and printed materials like posters and handouts that share security tips.
cards.explanation: Three parts: welcome people, teach them, remind them with posters.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness, Education, and Training Program”.

cards.question: A standard security awareness program should include, at a minimum, [[new user orientation]], [[lectures or computer-based trainings]] (CBTs), and [[printed materials]] like posters and handouts that share security tips.
cards.answer: A standard security awareness program should include, at a minimum, new user orientation, lectures or computer-based trainings (CBTs), and printed materials like posters and handouts that share security tips.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the orientation, the lessons, the printed materials.

cards.question: According to the manual, who is responsible for information security in a company?
cards.answer: Every person in the organization, even if small teams govern it.
cards.explanation: The specialists are few, but everyone is part of the defense.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1, start of the section on the awareness program.

cards.question: A poster says: “Lock your screen when you leave.” Is this more like awareness or like training?
options: Awareness
Training
cards.answer: Awareness
cards.explanation: A poster reminds you of a habit. It does not make you practice.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: the difference between awareness, education and training is a simplified explanation, not a sentence from the book.

cards.question: The director wants every employee to know the threats and to know how to handle them. What does she set up?
options: Orientation, lessons and posters
A penetration test and an audit
A new firewall and a new antivirus
One more backup per week
options_why: These checks test systems. They teach the employees nothing.
These tools protect machines, not the decisions people make.
A backup protects data, but it teaches the employees nothing.
cards.answer: Orientation, lessons and posters
cards.explanation: This is the minimum content of an awareness program: orientation, lessons and printed materials.

cards.question: What is part of the minimum content of a standard program?
cards.answer: In the minimum: orientation for new people, lessons or CBTs, posters and handouts. Outside the minimum: a new firewall, a vendor audit, a penetration test.
cards.explanation: The minimum is about people and messages. The other items are controls or tools.

cards.question: An awareness program includes at least an orientation for new people, lessons or [[CBTs]], and [[printed]] materials.
cards.answer: An awareness program includes at least an orientation for new people, lessons or CBTs, and printed materials.
cards.explanation: A welcome, lessons, reminders on paper.

cards.question: Why do people say that a company is only as secure as its weakest link?
cards.answer: The tools can be excellent, but an attacker only needs one person who gets tricked. The staff is often that link.
cards.explanation: One poorly informed person can open the door for everyone.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1. Security is only as strong as its weakest link, often the staff.

cards.question: What does CBT mean?
cards.answer: Computer-based training: a lesson you take on a computer.
cards.explanation: You have probably done one already: an online course with questions.

cards.question: What if a company does not organize any orientation for its new employees?
cards.answer: They do not know the threats or the good habits from day one. They become the weak link without knowing it.
cards.explanation: The orientation is the first contact with the company's security.

cards.question: You are a new employee. Write three things you expect to find in the company's awareness program.
cards.answer: An orientation when you arrive, lessons or CBTs, and posters or handouts with security tips.
cards.explanation: These are the three minimum parts named in the manual.

cards.question: What other techniques does the manual name to strengthen awareness?
cards.answer: Phishing and social engineering exercises, security champions and gamification.
cards.explanation: Each one has its own planet in this galaxy.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1, section “Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness, Education, and Training Program”.

decouverte.titre: The call from the fake technician
paragraphes: The phone rings in an office. A voice says: “Hello, I am from the IT department. I need your password.”
The voice is polite and a little rushed. The employee gives the password. No computer was hacked: a human was tricked.
Pretending to be someone else to get information is called social engineering.

decouverte.comme: To get into a locked building, someone does not break the door. He dresses up as a delivery person and politely asks you to open it.
decouverte.enVrai: Social engineering attacks the person, not the machine. The attacker pretends to be someone else to get sensitive data. Email is the favorite playground, and then we call it phishing. The picture stops here: a disguise can sometimes be spotted, but a tricky message can look perfect.

decouverte.question: Why does a firewall not stop an employee who gives a password over the phone?
options: It watches machines, not people
It is too old
It only looks at emails
decouverte.explanation: A firewall filters the traffic of machines. It cannot do anything against a person who talks. Its age or what it watches does not change that here.

decouverte.texte: Mia gets an email: “I am in a meeting. Quickly buy gift cards for a client.” The address looks like the director's. She clicks the link and types her password. This is phishing, the most common form of social engineering.
A company sends its employees a trap email on purpose: this is a simulated phishing exercise. Anyone who clicks gets a polite message and a training reminder. The goal is to learn, not to punish.

cards.question: Official definition: “social engineering”
cards.answer: Social engineering is the practice of human manipulation that involves an attacker pretending to be someone else in an effort to retrieve sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Key words: human manipulation, pretending to be someone else.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Social Engineering”.

cards.question: Social engineering is the practice of human [[manipulation]] that involves an attacker pretending to be someone else in an effort to retrieve [[sensitive]] data.
cards.answer: Social engineering is the practice of human manipulation that involves an attacker pretending to be someone else in an effort to retrieve sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Humans are manipulated to get sensitive data.

cards.question: Social engineering is the practice of [[human manipulation]] that involves an [[attacker pretending]] to be someone else in an effort to [[retrieve sensitive data]].
cards.answer: Social engineering is the practice of human manipulation that involves an attacker pretending to be someone else in an effort to retrieve sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the human manipulation, the attacker who pretends, the goal: the data.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “social engineering” from memory.
cards.answer: Social engineering is the practice of human manipulation that involves an attacker pretending to be someone else in an effort to retrieve sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: human manipulation, pretending to be someone else, getting the data.

cards.question: Official definition: “phishing”
cards.answer: Phishing is the most common form of social engineering, and it relates to social engineering activities that are conducted over email.
cards.explanation: Phishing = social engineering by email.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Social Engineering”.

cards.question: Phishing is the most [[common]] form of social engineering, and it relates to social engineering activities that are conducted over [[email]].
cards.answer: Phishing is the most common form of social engineering, and it relates to social engineering activities that are conducted over email.
cards.explanation: Two words: common (the most frequent) and email (the way it is done).

cards.question: Phishing is the [[most common form]] of social engineering, and it relates to [[social engineering activities]] that are [[conducted over email]].
cards.answer: Phishing is the most common form of social engineering, and it relates to social engineering activities that are conducted over email.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the most common form, social engineering, email.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “phishing” from memory.
cards.answer: Phishing is the most common form of social engineering, and it relates to social engineering activities that are conducted over email.
cards.explanation: Remember two ideas: the most common form, and email.

cards.question: Official definition: why phishing worries people so much
cards.answer: Phishing is routinely at the top of the most common security concerns because it can evade many of your most sophisticated security tools and compromise an organization's weakest link — its people.
cards.explanation: It gets around the tools and targets the people.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Social Engineering”.

cards.question: Phishing is routinely at the top of the most common security concerns because it can [[evade many]] of your most [[sophisticated security tools]] and compromise an organization's [[weakest link]] — its people.
cards.answer: Phishing is routinely at the top of the most common security concerns because it can evade many of your most sophisticated security tools and compromise an organization's weakest link — its people.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: it escapes the tools, even clever ones, and it targets the weakest link.

cards.question: Why does phishing stay at the top of the security concerns?
cards.answer: It can get around many clever security tools, and it targets the weakest link: the people.
cards.explanation: A good tool does not protect you from one unlucky click.

cards.question: A stranger calls an employee and pretends to be the IT department. Is this phishing?
options: No: it is not an email
Yes: every kind of social engineering is phishing
cards.answer: No: it is not an email
cards.explanation: Phishing is social engineering done by email. Here it is a phone call: it is social engineering, but not phishing.

cards.question: An employee clicks the link in a simulated phishing exercise. What should happen next?
options: The employee is told, then trained again
The employee is sent away the next day
Nothing: the exercise is over for that person
The account is blocked without any explanation
options_why: The goal is to learn, not to punish: the manual talks about extra training.
With no feedback, the employee will not know they were tricked, so nothing is learned.
Blocking without explaining does not teach anyone to spot phishing.
cards.answer: The employee is told, then trained again
cards.explanation: The manual says that anyone who clicks should be told. They take a refresher training: spotting and reporting phishing.

cards.question: Put the steps of simulated phishing exercises in order.
cards.answer:
1. Explain why phishing is dangerous and how to spot it
2. Launch simulated exercises at random
3. Find which types of phishing work and who needs help
4. Tell those who clicked and train them again
cards.explanation: First we educate, then we reinforce with exercises, then we analyze, then we help those who need it.

items: Explain why phishing is dangerous and how to spot it
Find which types of phishing work and who needs help
Tell those who clicked and train them again

cards.question: Phishing is a form of social engineering carried out by [[email|mail|e-mail]].
cards.answer: Phishing is a form of social engineering carried out by email.
cards.explanation: The way it is done is email, not the phone.

cards.question: Why launch simulated phishing exercises at random?
cards.answer: They reinforce the training and show where the risks are. They reveal which types of phishing work and who needs more training.
cards.explanation: A random exercise gives an honest picture of everyone's habits.

cards.question: What does the manual advise doing first, before the simulated exercises?
cards.answer: Explain to employees why phishing is dangerous and how to spot it.
cards.explanation: You do not test someone before teaching them.

cards.question: What if a company only runs simulated exercises and never explains phishing?
cards.answer: Employees get tricked without knowing why. The manual says to start by educating, then reinforce with exercises.
cards.explanation: A test with no lesson only shows the mistakes, without fixing them.

cards.question: You get an email that looks like phishing. What do you do, in the spirit of the manual?
cards.answer: I do not click, I try to spot the signs of phishing, and I report it.
cards.explanation: Spot and report: this is what the refresher training teaches.

paragraphes: In your school, the principal and the teachers cannot talk to every student every day. So there is a class representative.
He passes messages in both directions. Students listen to him because he is one of them.
In a company, the security team is small. It relies on a security champion, a coworker who passes on its messages.

decouverte.comme: The representative links the school office and the class. He is not a supervisor: he stays a student.
decouverte.enVrai: The security champion links the security team and the rest of the company. He encourages good habits in people whose main job is not security. The picture stops here: a class elects its representative, but the organization chooses its champion.

decouverte.question: At the start, which teams was the security champion role created for?
options: The teams that build software
The sales teams
The reception teams
decouverte.explanation: The role was born to raise awareness of application security, meaning the security of the company's software. Today, a champion can be named in any team outside security.

decouverte.texte: Karim works in accounting. He takes a training from the security team. Afterward, he reminds his coworkers to be careful with suspicious invoice emails. When someone has a doubt, he answers or tells the security team.

cards.question: Official definition: “security champion”
cards.answer: A security champion is a liaison between an organization's security team and the rest of the company; they are tasked with raising security awareness within the organization.
cards.explanation: Liaison = link, like the class representative.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Security Champions”.

cards.question: A security champion is a [[liaison]] between an organization's security team and the rest of the company; they are tasked with raising security [[awareness]] within the organization.
cards.answer: A security champion is a liaison between an organization's security team and the rest of the company; they are tasked with raising security awareness within the organization.
cards.explanation: Two words: liaison (the link) and awareness (knowing about risks).

cards.question: A security champion is a [[liaison between]] an organization's [[security team]] and the rest of the company; they are tasked with [[raising security awareness]] within the organization.
cards.answer: A security champion is a liaison between an organization's security team and the rest of the company; they are tasked with raising security awareness within the organization.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the link between, the security team, the mission of raising awareness.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “security champion” from memory.
cards.answer: A security champion is a liaison between an organization's security team and the rest of the company; they are tasked with raising security awareness within the organization.
cards.explanation: Two parts: the link between the team and the company, then the mission.

cards.question: Official definition: the role of a champion
cards.answer: In this role, a security champion is an advocate of security best practices for employees who don't work on security as their primary job.
cards.explanation: The champion talks to people who are not security specialists.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Security Champions”. Advocate means someone who speaks up for a cause.

cards.question: In this role, a [[security champion]] is an [[advocate of security best practices]] for employees who [[don't work on security]] as their primary job.
cards.answer: In this role, a security champion is an advocate of security best practices for employees who don't work on security as their primary job.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the champion, the role of advocate, the audience.

cards.question: Official definition: where the champion role comes from
cards.answer: The role of security champion was initially created to raise awareness of application security on software development teams, but nowadays, organizations may frequently choose to assign a security champion to any (or all) nonsecurity teams.
cards.explanation: First for developers, today for any team outside security.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Security Champions”.

cards.question: The role of security champion was [[initially created]] to raise awareness of [[application security]] on software development teams, but nowadays, organizations may frequently choose to assign a security champion to [[any (or all) nonsecurity teams]].
cards.answer: The role of security champion was initially created to raise awareness of application security on software development teams, but nowadays, organizations may frequently choose to assign a security champion to any (or all) nonsecurity teams.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: at the start, application security, and today every team outside security.

cards.question: For which employees does a champion promote good security practices?
cards.answer: For employees whose main job is not security.
cards.explanation: The specialists already know: the champion talks to the others.

cards.question: An accounting employee passes on the security team's tips. Can she be a security champion?
options: Yes, if she was given that role
No, only IT people can
cards.answer: Yes, if she was given that role
cards.explanation: Today, an organization can name a champion in any team that does not work on security.

cards.question: The security team has four people, the company has four hundred. What can it do so that everyone gets the messages?
options: Name champions in the other teams
Replace the messages with a firewall
Forbid the other teams to talk about security
Wait for the next incident
options_why: A firewall does not send any message to people.
The opposite: we want awareness to spread everywhere.
Waiting for the incident means acting too late.
cards.answer: Name champions in the other teams
cards.explanation: Champions link the small security team and the rest of the company.

cards.question: The champion role was first created for the security of [[applications]] in development teams.
cards.answer: The champion role was first created for the security of applications in development teams.
cards.explanation: Developers build the software: their choices affect the whole company.

cards.question: Why is a champion useful to a small security team?
cards.answer: The champion links the team with the other teams and repeats good habits close to coworkers. The security team cannot talk to everyone every day.
cards.explanation: A message from a nearby coworker is often listened to more.

cards.question: What if every team in the company had a security champion?
cards.answer: The manual says a champion can be named in any team, or in all of them. Awareness then reaches everywhere, not only the specialists.
cards.explanation: The more relays there are, the more messages get through.

cards.question: You are the security champion of your class. Write what you do for your classmates.
cards.answer: I link them with the security team. I repeat the good practices to my classmates and help them stay alert.
cards.explanation: Your role: pass on, explain, encourage.

paragraphes: You learn a language with an app. It gives you points, levels, and a message when you keep a streak of days without a break.
You are not really playing a game. Still, you want to come back every day.
Using game techniques to make people want to learn is called gamification.

decouverte.comme: In sports, the scoreboard makes you want to improve, even in practice.
decouverte.enVrai: Gamification borrows points, levels and challenges from games. It uses them in activities that are not games. In security, it helps employees learn good habits with pleasure. The picture stops here: the goal is not to win, but to learn.

decouverte.question: A company offers a security quiz with points and a ranking. Is it a real video game?
options: No: these are game techniques in an activity that is not a game
Yes: it is a full game
We cannot know
decouverte.answer: No: these are game techniques in an activity that is not a game
decouverte.explanation: The quiz is not a game: it borrows game techniques to interest and educate people. This is what the manual calls gamification.

decouverte.texte: Every month, a company launches a small challenge: spot trap emails. Teams win points and badges. The manual says that this kind of game can educate employees in an interesting and engaging way.

cards.question: Official definition: “gamification”
cards.answer: Gamification is the use of game techniques in nongame applications to engage and educate an audience.
cards.explanation: Game techniques, but in an activity that is not a game.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Gamification”. The word comes from “game”: the idea is to borrow what makes games fun.

cards.question: Gamification is the use of game [[techniques]] in nongame applications to engage and [[educate]] an audience.
cards.answer: Gamification is the use of game techniques in nongame applications to engage and educate an audience.
cards.explanation: Two words: techniques (of games) and educate (teach).

cards.question: Gamification is the [[use of game techniques]] in [[nongame applications]] to [[engage and educate]] an audience.
cards.answer: Gamification is the use of game techniques in nongame applications to engage and educate an audience.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: using game techniques, outside of games, to captivate and educate.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “gamification” from memory.
cards.answer: Gamification is the use of game techniques in nongame applications to engage and educate an audience.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: game techniques, applications that are not games, engage and educate.

cards.question: Official definition: gamification in awareness
cards.answer: In security awareness, gamification can provide a fun and engaging way to educate employees and promote strong security practices.
cards.explanation: A fun way to learn good habits.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Gamification”.

cards.question: In [[security awareness]], gamification can provide a [[fun and engaging way]] to educate employees and [[promote strong security practices]].
cards.answer: In security awareness, gamification can provide a fun and engaging way to educate employees and promote strong security practices.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: awareness, a fun way, good practices.

cards.question: What does “nongame applications” mean in the definition of gamification?
cards.answer: Activities that are not games, like security training.
cards.explanation: We borrow the methods of games, not their goal.

cards.question: Which of these two situations is gamification?
options: A security training with points and levels
A video game sold in stores
cards.answer: A security training with points and levels
cards.explanation: Gamification puts game techniques into an activity that is not a game. A video game is already a game.

cards.question: Employees ignore the online security course. Which idea uses gamification?
options: Give points and a ranking
Make the course required and longer
Send a reminder email every day
Cut the course in half
options_why: Forcing people and making it longer uses no game technique.
A daily reminder is nothing like a game and can be annoying.
Cutting removes content without making the course more attractive.
cards.answer: Give points and a ranking
cards.explanation: Points, levels and rankings are game techniques that make people want to take part.

cards.question: Gamification means using [[game]] techniques in activities that are not games.
cards.answer: Gamification means using game techniques in activities that are not games.
cards.explanation: Games give us points and levels. Gamification borrows them to help people learn.

cards.question: Why can gamification help people learn security rules?
cards.answer: Because a game makes learning interesting and engaging. Employees want to take part, so they practice good habits more often.
cards.explanation: We learn more willingly what is fun.

cards.question: What is the double goal of gamification, according to its definition?
cards.answer: To engage, which means to captivate, and to educate the audience.
cards.explanation: If the game is fun but teaches nothing, it does only half of its job.

cards.question: What if the game is fun but teaches no security concept?
cards.answer: It does not do its job. The manual says these games must educate employees on critical security concepts.
cards.explanation: Being fun is not enough: people must also learn something.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1, section “Gamification”.

cards.question: Invent a small game to teach employees how to spot phishing.
cards.answer: For example: a timed quiz where you sort emails into safe or trap, with points and a ranking.
cards.explanation: Points, a challenge and a learning goal: this is gamification.

paragraphes: Your brother lends you a travel guide that is ten years old. It lists a restaurant that has closed and a road that no longer exists.
You get lost, because the world changed and the guide did not.
A security training program can get old in the same way. To avoid that, we read it again regularly: these are the periodic content reviews.

decouverte.titre: The guide that gets a new edition
decouverte.comme: A good travel guide gets a new edition every year, with the new restaurants and the new roads.
decouverte.enVrai: The content of the security course must be read again and updated at least once a year. Threats keep changing, so the content must change too. The picture stops here: some security content must change even more often.

decouverte.question: A company has reused the same security course for five years. What is the main risk?
options: It talks about technologies and threats that are out of date
It costs too much to print
Employees know it by heart
decouverte.answer: It talks about technologies and threats that are out of date
decouverte.explanation: Threats and weaknesses keep changing. An old course misses the new ones. Employees knowing it by heart would not be a problem if it were up to date.

decouverte.titre: A course that still talks about floppy disks
decouverte.texte: A security course still tells people to be careful with floppy disks. It says nothing about very well made trick emails. A yearly review would have removed the old terms. It would have added the current threats of the organization and its industry.

cards.question: Official definition: periodic content reviews
cards.answer: Content should be reviewed and updated annually, at a minimum, to ensure that there is no reference to obsolete or irrelevant technologies or terminology, and these reviews should validate that all security awareness and training materials reflect current security trends, concepts, and concerns that are relevant to your organization and industry.
cards.explanation: At least every year: remove what is old, add what is current.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Periodic Content Reviews”. Obsolete means out of date, no longer used.

cards.question: Content should be reviewed and updated [[annually, at a minimum]], to ensure that there is [[no reference to obsolete]] or irrelevant technologies or terminology, and these reviews should validate that all security awareness and training materials reflect [[current security trends]], concepts, and concerns that are relevant to your organization and industry.
cards.answer: Content should be reviewed and updated annually, at a minimum, to ensure that there is no reference to obsolete or irrelevant technologies or terminology, and these reviews should validate that all security awareness and training materials reflect current security trends, concepts, and concerns that are relevant to your organization and industry.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the minimum frequency, removing what is old, reflecting current trends.

cards.question: Official definition: “live” content
cards.answer: Ideally, security awareness content should be considered "live" material that evolves even more frequently than these periodic reviews.
cards.explanation: “Live”: living content, which moves between two reviews.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Periodic Content Reviews”.

cards.question: Ideally, [[security awareness content]] should be considered "live" material that [[evolves even more frequently]] than these [[periodic reviews]].
cards.answer: Ideally, security awareness content should be considered "live" material that evolves even more frequently than these periodic reviews.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the awareness content, it changes more often, than the periodic reviews.

cards.question: What is the minimum frequency for reading again and updating awareness content?
cards.answer: At least once a year.
cards.explanation: This is a minimum: you can do it more often.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1, section “Periodic Content Reviews”: annually, at a minimum.

cards.question: Two companies review their training. Which one follows the manual's ideal?
options: The one that also updates between reviews
The one that touches nothing between reviews
cards.answer: The one that also updates between reviews
cards.explanation: The manual wants “live” content, which changes even more often than the periodic reviews.

cards.question: During the yearly review, you find a course that talks about a tool nobody uses anymore. What do you do?
options: I remove that part and update it
I keep it: it is still true
I wait for next year's review
I delete the whole course at once
options_why: A mention of a tool nobody uses does not help anyone anymore.
The point of the review is to fix things now.
Deleting the whole course takes away what is still useful.
cards.answer: I remove that part and update it
cards.explanation: The review is there to remove what is old and to reflect current trends.

cards.question: After a review, what do we remove and what do we keep?
cards.answer: To remove or update: advice about an abandoned technology, forgotten vocabulary, an example from another industry. To keep: advice that is still valid, a current trend, a current concern.
cards.explanation: We keep what is current and useful to the organization, we remove what is out of date.

items.text: Advice about a technology nobody uses anymore
Vocabulary that is no longer used
An example that no longer fits your industry
Advice that is still valid and useful to the company
A current security trend in your industry
A current concern of the organization

cards.question: The content must be read again and updated [[annually|every year|once a year]] at a minimum.
cards.answer: The content must be read again and updated annually at a minimum.
cards.explanation: Once a year, at least.

cards.question: Why read the awareness content again, even if it was good last year?
cards.answer: Because threats and weaknesses keep changing. Content that does not change ends up talking about things that are out of date.
cards.explanation: A good course from yesterday can become an incomplete course today.

cards.question: What should the content reviews validate, according to the manual?
cards.answer: That all materials reflect current security trends, concepts and concerns that matter to the organization and its industry.
cards.explanation: The content must fit the reality of your company and your industry.

cards.question: What if the content is treated as “live” material?
cards.answer: It is updated often, even between two reviews. It keeps up better with threats that change.
cards.explanation: Living content reacts quickly to what is new.

cards.question: Write three questions to ask yourself during a yearly content review.
cards.answer: Are there technologies or words that are out of date? Do the materials reflect current trends? Are they useful to our organization and our industry?
cards.explanation: These three questions follow the points named in the manual.

cards.question: According to the manual, who must make sure the training has the useful, current information?
cards.answer: You, as a CISSP. You must make sure the training has everything employees need to know.
cards.explanation: This is a responsibility of the security professional.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1, section “Periodic Content Reviews”, last sentence.

paragraphes: Your math teacher spent a month explaining fractions. He spoke well, and everyone listened. But did anyone understand?
He gives a small quiz. Many students miss the same question. He understands that he must explain that point again.
In a company, giving security courses is not enough: you must measure if they work. This is the program effectiveness evaluation.

decouverte.comme: A report card is not there to punish. It shows where help is needed.
decouverte.enVrai: Measuring how well an awareness program works helps find its weak points, not judge people. We look at the numbers, the quizzes, the opinions of employees and the reports they send. The picture stops here: we grade the program, not the students.

decouverte.question: In a security quiz, half of the employees miss the same question. What should we conclude?
options: The content may be unclear on this topic
These employees do not want to learn
The quiz is too easy
decouverte.answer: The content may be unclear on this topic
decouverte.explanation: If many employees make a mistake on the same topic, clearer information is probably needed. We improve the program, we do not blame people.

decouverte.titre: More reports is a good sign
decouverte.texte: After a training, a company gets twice as many messages from coworkers who report suspicious emails. This may sound worrying. Still, it is a good sign: employees are more alert. More reports is better than more successful attacks.

cards.question: Official definition: evaluating how well awareness activities work
cards.answer: Conducting security awareness, education, and training activities is not enough; it's equally important to evaluate and measure the effectiveness of your security education activities.
cards.explanation: Doing is not enough: you must also measure if it works.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Program Effectiveness Evaluation”.

cards.question: Conducting security awareness, education, and training activities is not [[enough]]; it's equally important to evaluate and [[measure]] the effectiveness of your security education activities.
cards.answer: Conducting security awareness, education, and training activities is not enough; it's equally important to evaluate and measure the effectiveness of your security education activities.
cards.explanation: Two words: enough and measure.

cards.question: Conducting security awareness, education, and training activities is [[not enough]]; it's [[equally important]] to [[evaluate and measure]] the effectiveness of your security education activities.
cards.answer: Conducting security awareness, education, and training activities is not enough; it's equally important to evaluate and measure the effectiveness of your security education activities.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: it is not enough, it is equally important, evaluate and measure.

cards.question: Write from memory the official sentence about evaluating awareness activities.
cards.answer: Conducting security awareness, education, and training activities is not enough; it's equally important to evaluate and measure the effectiveness of your security education activities.
cards.explanation: Two parts: it is not enough, it is equally important to evaluate and measure.

cards.question: Official definition: “training metrics”
cards.answer: Simple metrics like training completion rates are a great place to start when evaluating the effectiveness of your security awareness program.
cards.explanation: Counting who finished the training: the easiest way to start.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Program Effectiveness Evaluation”. Metrics means measurements, numbers you keep track of.

cards.question: [[Simple metrics]] like training completion rates are a [[great place to start]] when [[evaluating the effectiveness]] of your security awareness program.
cards.answer: Simple metrics like training completion rates are a great place to start when evaluating the effectiveness of your security awareness program.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: simple metrics, a good starting point, evaluating the effectiveness.

cards.question: Official definition: “quizzes”
cards.answer: Quizzes are most reliable when measuring the effectiveness of security policies and related information.
cards.explanation: A quiz mostly tests the policies and the information linked to them.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Program Effectiveness Evaluation”.

cards.question: Quizzes are [[most reliable]] when measuring the effectiveness of [[security policies]] and [[related information]].
cards.answer: Quizzes are most reliable when measuring the effectiveness of security policies and related information.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the most reliable, the security policies, the related information.

cards.question: Official definition: security awareness days or weeks
cards.answer: By sponsoring security awareness days or weeks, you not only have an opportunity to provide security education, but you can also use this as an opportunity to solicit feedback from your employees on the program itself.
cards.explanation: Educate, and at the same time ask for the employees' opinion.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Program Effectiveness Evaluation”. The manual talks about anonymous questionnaires.

cards.question: By sponsoring [[security awareness days or weeks]], you not only have an opportunity to provide security education, but you can also use this as an opportunity to [[solicit feedback]] from your employees on [[the program itself]].
cards.answer: By sponsoring security awareness days or weeks, you not only have an opportunity to provide security education, but you can also use this as an opportunity to solicit feedback from your employees on the program itself.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the days, collecting opinions, about the program itself.

cards.question: Official definition: “inherent” evaluation through reports
cards.answer: Certain metrics, such as the number of phishing emails and other security issues reported to IT, can provide a great deal of insight into the effectiveness of your program.
cards.explanation: The number of reports shows if employees remembered the good habits.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Program Effectiveness Evaluation”. Inherent means we look at the general state of security, with no separate test.

cards.question: Certain metrics, such as the number of [[phishing emails]] and other security issues [[reported to IT]], can provide a great deal of [[insight into the effectiveness]] of your program.
cards.answer: Certain metrics, such as the number of phishing emails and other security issues reported to IT, can provide a great deal of insight into the effectiveness of your program.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the phishing emails, reported to IT, what this says about effectiveness.

cards.question: Which evaluation method matches each example?
cards.answer: Training completion rates: the percentage of employees who finished the course. Quizzes: many mistakes on the same question, a test on the password policy. Awareness days: an anonymous questionnaire, a security week. Inherent evaluation: the number of suspicious emails reported.
cards.explanation: Each method looks at a different clue: completion, knowledge, opinion or behavior.

items.text: The percentage of employees who finished the course
Many employees make a mistake on the same question
A test result on the password policy
An anonymous questionnaire given to participants
A security week where opinions are collected
The number of suspicious emails reported to IT

cards.question: Only 30 percent of employees took the online course. Which method showed it?
options: Completion rates
A quiz on the security rules
An anonymous satisfaction questionnaire
The number of suspicious emails reported
options_why: A quiz measures what people remembered, not how many took the course.
A questionnaire collects opinions, not the number of participants.
Reports show the habits of employees, not whether they took the course.
cards.answer: Completion rates
cards.explanation: Completion rates tell you if the training reaches enough employees. They also show if you need a different way to deliver it.

cards.question: After the training, the number of suspicious emails reported goes up. Is this more of a good or a bad sign?
options: A good sign
A bad sign
cards.answer: A good sign
cards.explanation: Employees spot more suspicious emails and talk about them. More reports is better than more successful compromises.

cards.question: It is better to see [[reports]] of suspicious problems go up than successful [[compromises|attacks|break-ins]].
cards.answer: It is better to see reports of suspicious problems go up than successful compromises.
cards.explanation: An employee who reports has spotted the danger before it succeeds.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, domain 1, section “Program Effectiveness Evaluation”.

cards.question: Why can a quiz show that the course content must change?
cards.answer: If many employees miss the same question, clearer information is probably needed on that topic.
cards.explanation: A common mistake often comes from the course, not from the people.

cards.question: What do we measure with training completion rates?
cards.answer: Whether the training resources reach enough employees. They can also show that other ways of delivering are needed.
cards.explanation: This is the simplest measure to start with.

cards.question: Besides educating, why organize security awareness days or weeks?
cards.answer: To collect the opinion of employees on the program, for example with anonymous questionnaires.
cards.explanation: Employees say what works and what is boring.

cards.question: What if a company only looks at overall security, with no formal evaluation of the program?
cards.answer: It can get an idea of how well things work. The manual also asks for a formal evaluation, which targets the weak points of the program itself.
cards.explanation: Overall security depends on many things: we want to isolate how good the program is.

cards.question: You lead the security training of a company. Write two ways to know if it works.
cards.answer: For example: a quiz whose mistakes you analyze, and tracking the reports of suspicious emails.
cards.explanation: One measures what people know, the other what they do.
